html:
The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art is a Chinese book of mathematics, put together by many scholars over several centuries and reaching its final form in the Han dynasty, around the 1st century CE. It was the core of mathematical education in East Asia for over a thousand years.

It is a book of 246 practical problems, each with an answer and a method: measuring fields, sharing grain, paying taxes, digging canals, building walls. Its chapters cover areas and volumes, proportions, square and cube roots, right triangles and systems of linear equations.

Some of its methods were far ahead of their time. It solves systems of equations with a method like the one Europe later named Gaussian elimination, laid out with counting rods on a board, and it uses negative numbers, red and black rods for positive and negative. Unlike Euclid's Elements, it seeks general methods rather than proofs. The mathematician Liu Hui wrote a famous commentary on it in 263 CE.
